Cell Division & the Cell Cycle

Why cells divide, and the three kinds of division side by side: binary fission, mitosis and meiosis, and who does each. Then this module goes in depth on the two that copy DNA, binary fission and mitosis, with the cell cycle, haploid and diploid, and the human karyotype. Meiosis, the division that mixes DNA, gets its own deep dive in Module 3.2.

MODULE 3.1 · PART 1

Why cells divide, and binary fission

THE QUESTION Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. What are the two jobs of every division, where is the DNA, and how do prokaryotes divide?

In this part, following the lecture: why cells divide, replication then segregation, prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes and where the DNA is, the three kinds of division at a glance, and binary fission step by step.

START HERE

Why do cells divide?

Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. Cell division is how one cell becomes two, and there are several reasons a living thing needs it.

INTERACTIVE · FOUR SCENES

One process, four jobs

Tap a button to explore
1 · ONE-CELLED ORGANISMSDivision is reproductionFor a unicellular organism, such as a bacterium or a yeast, dividing in two is making offspring. Each daughter cell is a new organism.
2 · DEVELOPMENT AND GROWTHFrom one cell to a whole bodyYou started as a single cell, a fertilized egg. Mitosis turned it into the trillions of cells you are made of, and growth still depends on it.
3 · REPAIR AND REGENERATIONReplacing what is lostScrape your knee and the cells around the wound divide to fill the gap. Your body also keeps replacing worn-out skin cells, blood cells and the cells lining your gut.
4 · ASEXUAL REPRODUCTIONA new organism from one parentSome multicellular species reproduce asexually by mitosis. A strawberry plant sends out a runner that grows into a new plant with the same DNA.
TAP A SCENEAt least three reasonsCells divide for reproduction, for development and growth, and for repair and regeneration. Tap each scene.
REPRODUCTIONMake a new organismOne-celled organisms, and some multicellular species that reproduce asexually.
GROWTHBuild a bodyDevelopment from one fertilized egg into an adult.
REPAIRFix and replaceHealing wounds and replacing worn-out cells.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Unicellular

Made of a single cell. For a unicellular organism, cell division is reproduction.

COPY, THEN SHARE

Replication, then segregation

Whatever the reason, and whatever kind of cell, every cell division has the same two parts. First the cell copies its DNA. Then it hands one copy to each daughter cell.

INTERACTIVE · ONE CELL BECOMES TWO

Copy, then share

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
STARTOne cell, one set of DNAThe parent cell has its DNA. To make two complete cells, it needs two complete copies.
PART 1 · REPLICATIONCopy the DNAThe cell replicates its DNA: it makes an exact copy of every DNA molecule. The two copies stay joined for now.
PART 2 · SEGREGATIONSend one copy to each daughter cellThe copies are segregated, pulled apart into two daughter cells. Each daughter gets one full copy.
THREE KINDS OF DIVISION, SAME TWO JOBSBinary fission, mitosis and meiosis all replicate the DNA and then segregate the copies. What differs is who does each one, where the DNA is, and what comes out. They are side by side a little further down.
COMMON MIX-UPReplication and segregation are not the same thing. Replication makes the copies. Segregation separates the copies into different cells. A cell that replicated but did not segregate would just have twice the DNA.
WHO'S WHO, AND WHERE THE DNA IS

Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes

Every living thing belongs to one of three domains. Two of them, bacteria and archaea, are prokaryotes; the third is the eukaryotes. Which group an organism is in tells you where its DNA is and how its cells divide.

INTERACTIVE · THE TREE OF LIFE

Three domains, and what each one does

Tap a button to explore
BACTERIA · PROKARYOTESOne cell, no nucleusBacteria such as E. coli are always unicellular. Their DNA is one circular chromosome, often with plasmids, with no nucleus around it.They reproduce by binary fission, which is asexual, and can pass DNA to each other by conjugation.
ARCHAEA · PROKARYOTESLook like bacteria, related to usArchaea (for example the microbes that make methane in swamps and cow stomachs) are also unicellular prokaryotes with circular DNA, and also divide by binary fission.On the tree, though, archaea are the closest relatives of eukaryotes. For cell division, treat bacteria and archaea as one group: prokaryotes.
EUKARYA · EUKARYOTESA nucleus, and one cell or manyEukaryotes keep their linear chromosomes in a nucleus. Some are unicellular (yeast, amoebas); others are multicellular (animals, plants, most fungi).Their cells divide by mitosis, and the germ cells of sexually reproducing species also divide by meiosis.
ALL THREEThe mind mapProkaryotes (bacteria, archaea): one cell, no nucleus, binary fission. Eukaryotes: a nucleus, mitosis and meiosis. The rest of this section zooms in on where the DNA sits.
TAP A DOMAINThe tree of lifeThree branches from one common ancestor. Tap a domain to see what it does.
UNICELLULAR · ONE CELLMULTICELLULAR · MANY CELLS
WhoAll bacteria and archaea; some eukaryotes: yeast, amoebas, Paramecium, many algaeOnly eukaryotes: animals, plants, most fungi (mushrooms, molds), seaweeds such as kelp
One cell divisionMakes a new organism: division is reproductionMakes more cells in the same body, for growth and repair
ReproductionBinary fission (prokaryotes) or mitosis (yeast, amoebas)Asexual, by mitosis (runners, budding), or sexual, by meiosis and fertilization
INTERACTIVE · WHERE, WHAT SHAPE, AND HOW IT FITS

Where is the DNA?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
WHERE · PROKARYOTESOne place: loose in the cellA bacterium or archaeon has no nucleus. Its DNA sits in the cytoplasm, held on the cell membrane. Almost all its genes are on one circular chromosome.Plasmids are small extra circles of DNA, usually with genes that are not essential, such as one for resisting an antibiotic.
WHERE · EUKARYOTESThree places, two shapesThe nucleus holds most of the DNA, as linear chromosomes: this is the nuclear DNA, what "genome" usually means.Mitochondria, and the chloroplasts of plants and algae, each hold their own small circle of DNA. They came from bacteria long ago by endosymbiosis (Module 2.2), which is why their DNA is circular and they still divide by binary fission.
HOW IT FITS · ZOOM INNucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene: one inside the otherThese are not four separate places. They are zoom levels of the same thing.The nucleus holds the chromosomes. A chromosome is the name for one long double-stranded DNA molecule together with the proteins it is wound on. In a cell, DNA is always on its proteins; only how tightly it is packed changes. A gene is one stretch of that DNA, and one chromosome carries many genes.
OVER TIME · THE CELL CYCLESame DNA, different packingStages change how the DNA is packed, not where it is. Between divisions (interphase) the chromosomes are long, loose threads, so genes can be read and the DNA copied.Before the cell divides they condense: each molecule coils up into a short, compact chromosome that is easy to move. Part 2 follows this step by step.
PROKARYOTES (BACTERIA, ARCHAEA)EUKARYOTES
NucleusNone, and no other compartmentsYes, plus other compartments
ChromosomesOne, circularUsually several, linear
Extra DNAPlasmids: small, usually non-essential genesCircular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts
DNA attached toThe cell membraneNot the membrane: inside the nucleus
How they divideBinary fissionMitosis (body cells) and meiosis (germ cells)
COMMON MIX-UPThe circle of DNA in a mitochondrion is not in the nucleus. Each mitochondrion (and each chloroplast) keeps its own small circular DNA inside itself, just as the bacterium it came from kept its DNA with no nucleus around it. A plant cell keeps DNA in three places: linear chromosomes in the nucleus, a small circle in each mitochondrion, a small circle in each chloroplast. And mitochondria and chloroplasts have no plasmids: plasmids belong to bacteria and archaea.
WHY DO BACTERIA HAVE PLASMIDS AS WELL AS A CHROMOSOME?Think of a core manual plus optional add-on cards. The chromosome carries the essential genes, everything the cell needs to live. Plasmids are small extra circles with genes that are usually not essential, such as one for resisting an antibiotic. A plasmid is copied along with the cell's DNA and handed to the daughter cells, and it can also be passed to a neighbor by conjugation. So a useful gene can be gained, lost or shared without touching the essential ones. That is also why biologists use plasmids to copy genes in the lab (DNA Manipulation).
Check yourself: Why do mitochondria and chloroplasts contain circular DNA?

Because they were once free-living bacteria. An ancestral cell engulfed them (endosymbiosis, Module 2.2), and they kept the circular DNA bacteria have. They still divide by binary fission.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Multicellular

Made of many cells, like animals, plants and most fungi. Only eukaryotes are multicellular. Cell division builds and repairs the body; reproduction is a separate job.

Plasmid

A small circle of DNA in a prokaryotic cell, separate from the chromosome. It usually carries genes that are not essential for the species.

Chromosome

One double-stranded DNA molecule packaged with proteins. It carries many genes. After S phase it is two sister chromatids, but it still counts as one chromosome.

Nuclear DNA

The DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, organized into linear chromosomes. In eukaryotes, "genome" usually means the nuclear DNA.

WHO DOES WHICH?

Binary fission, mitosis and meiosis

There are three kinds of cell division. Which one a cell uses depends on whether it is a prokaryote or a eukaryote, and, in eukaryotes, on whether it is a body cell or a germ cell.

THREE KINDS OF ORGANISM

Who divides how?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
PROKARYOTES · BACTERIA AND ARCHAEABinary fission, and that's itA bacterium or an archaeon is unicellular: one cell is the whole organism. To reproduce, it copies its DNA and splits in two by binary fission. That is asexual reproduction: one parent, two identical offspring.Prokaryotes have no nucleus and never do mitosis or meiosis.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE SEXUALLYMitosis and meiosis in the same bodyIn an animal or a flowering plant, the somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis: 2 identical cells, for growth and repair. Only the germ cells (in ovaries and testes, or in flowers) divide by meiosis: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes, all different.Here mitosis is not reproduction. Reproduction is meiosis (to make gametes) plus fertilization, a gamete from each of two parents.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE ASEXUALLYMitosis only, no meiosisMany eukaryotes also make offspring by mitosis alone: yeast grows buds, a strawberry plant sends out runners, and female aphids have young without mating. One parent, no mate, and the offspring are clones.Many species do both, depending on conditions (strawberries also flower). So prokaryotes are always asexual, but eukaryotes can be asexual, sexual or both.
COMMON MIX-UPMitosis vs. meiosis is not just about where it happens. Yes, mitosis is in body cells and meiosis only in germ cells. But they are different processes with different results: mitosis gives 2 identical cells (2n → 2n); meiosis gives 4 different gametes with half the chromosomes (2n → n).
COMMON MIX-UPProkaryotes = asexual, but eukaryotes ≠ always sexual. Binary fission is always asexual. Eukaryotes can reproduce asexually by mitosis (yeast, strawberries), sexually by meiosis and fertilization (people), or both.
INTERACTIVE · SIDE BY SIDE

Three kinds of division

Tap a button to explore
BINARY FISSION · PROKARYOTESBacteria and archaeaWho: prokaryotes, which are bacteria and archaea (for cell division they work the same way). Also mitochondria and chloroplasts inside eukaryotic cells, because they descend from bacteria (endosymbiosis, Module 2.2).The DNA: one circular chromosome (plus plasmids), no nucleus, attached to the cell membrane.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent. For a one-celled prokaryote, that is reproduction.
MITOSIS · EUKARYOTESSomatic (body) cellsWho: eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists), in their somatic (body) cells. In a eukaryote that reproduces asexually, mitosis is also how it makes offspring.The DNA: several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent (2n → 2n), for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
MEIOSIS · EUKARYOTESGerm cells onlyWho: eukaryotes that reproduce sexually, and only in germ cells, the cells that make eggs and sperm. The same organism does mitosis in all its other cells: that is why the dashed box joins the two.Two divisions in a row: meiosis I splits each homologous pair (A from a) into 2 cells; meiosis II splits the sister chromatids, like mitosis, into 4 gametes. No DNA copying in between.The DNA: linear chromosomes in a nucleus, in homologous pairs (A from the mother, a from the father).Result: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes (2n → n) and different DNA, for sexual reproduction. How it works is Module 3.2.
ALL THREETwo categories, same two jobsBinary fission is its own category (prokaryotes). Mitosis and meiosis belong together (eukaryotes). Each one replicates the DNA and then segregates the copies. Binary fission segregates by the cell growing; mitosis and meiosis need a spindle to pull chromosomes apart.
TAP ONEWhich cells do which?Prokaryotes do only binary fission. Eukaryotes do mitosis and meiosis, never binary fission (except inside their mitochondria and chloroplasts).
BINARY FISSIONProkaryotesBacteria and archaea · circular chromosome, no nucleus · 2 identical cells · reproduction
MITOSISEukaryote body cellsLinear chromosomes in a nucleus · 2 identical cells · 2n → 2n · growth, repair, asexual reproduction
MEIOSISEukaryote germ cells onlyLinear chromosomes in a nucleus · 4 different gametes · 2n → n · sexual reproduction
COMMON MIX-UPMeiosis I and meiosis II are not generations. They are two divisions in a row inside one meiosis: 1 germ cell → 2 cells (meiosis I, homologous pairs separate) → 4 gametes (meiosis II, sister chromatids separate). The next generation only starts at fertilization. Module 3.2 goes through both step by step.
COMMON MIX-UPBacteria never do mitosis or meiosis. Prokaryotes divide only by binary fission. Mitosis and meiosis happen only in eukaryotes: mitosis gives 2 identical cells, meiosis gives 4 gametes with different DNA.
Check yourself: What results from mitosis, and how could a mutation change that?

Two daughter cells with the same DNA as the parent. A mutation, a change that happens by chance when the DNA is copied, makes the copies differ slightly, so a daughter cell can carry a new mutation the parent cell did not have.

COMMON MIX-UPBinary fission is not a kind of meiosis. It is the prokaryote way of making identical copies, like mitosis. Bacteria recombine DNA by conjugation, which is not cell division at all.
Check yourself: Do bacteria shuffle their DNA the way humans do in meiosis?

No. Bacteria never do meiosis. They can share DNA by conjugation, passing a copy of a plasmid or other DNA to a neighbor, which also creates new combinations of genes. But it happens apart from reproduction: binary fission itself just copies.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Mitosis

Division of the nucleus in which the sister chromatids of every chromosome are pulled apart, so each daughter cell gets the same DNA as the parent cell.

Meiosis

The cell division that turns a diploid cell into four haploid gametes, whose DNA is different from the parent cell's.

Conjugation

A way prokaryotes share DNA: one cell passes a copy of some of its DNA, often a plasmid, to another cell through a connecting bridge. No new cell is made, so it is not reproduction.

HOW PROKARYOTES DIVIDE

Binary fission, step by step

Bacteria and archaea divide by binary fission. It has the same two jobs, replication and segregation, and it is the simplest way to do them.

INTERACTIVE · SIX STEPS

One bacterium becomes two

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
1 · BEFOREDNA attached to the membraneThe circular chromosome is one DNA molecule: two strands twisted around each other, joined end to end in a circle. A protein holds it to the inside of the cell membrane.
2 · REPLICATION BEGINSCopying runs both ways roundReplication starts at one spot on the circle, the origin of replication, and runs in both directions around it.The growing copy (light) gets its own protein, attached to the membrane right next to the first one: two attachment sites, close together.
3 · COPIEDTwo circles, side by sideWhen the two copying points meet on the far side, there are two whole circles, each attached to the membrane near the other.Strictly, each circle is one original strand plus one new strand, with the same sequence. The two colors just let you follow the two circles.
4 · SEGREGATION BY GROWTHThe cell lengthensAs the cell grows longer, the two attachment sites move apart, carrying the two circles to opposite ends. Growth itself does the separating.
5 · CONSTRICTIONPinching in at the middleWhen the cell is about twice its original size and the circles are well apart, a ring of the protein FtsZ forms at the midpoint and the cell pinches in there.
6 · DIVISIONTwo daughter cellsNew membrane and cell wall are built across the middle, separating two daughter cells. Each has a complete copy of the DNA: the same genetic material as the parent cell.
WHAT SETS THE SPEED?Binary fission is regulated by nutrient availability. With plenty of nutrients, a bacterium copies its DNA and divides quickly. When nutrients run short, division slows down or stops.
NOT ONLY BACTERIAMitochondria and chloroplasts also divide by binary fission inside your cells, the way the bacteria they came from did. They got there by endosymbiosis (Module 2.2).
GO DEEPER · FROM THE TEXTBOOKFtsZ, the protein that rings the middle of a dividing bacterium, is related to tubulin, the protein of the spindle fibers in eukaryotes. And some one-celled eukaryotes, the dinoflagellates, divide halfway between the two ways: their nuclear envelope stays intact and their DNA is attached to it, so the nucleus grows and splits much like a bacterium. Forms like this suggest mitosis evolved from binary fission.
Check yourself: Why can a bacterium or archaeon separate its DNA just by growing, when a eukaryotic cell cannot?

Because a bacterium's DNA is attached to the cell membrane. As the cell grows, the membrane carries the two copies apart. A eukaryotic cell's DNA is inside a nucleus, not on the membrane, so it needs another way to pull the copies apart: mitosis.

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Cells divide to reproduce, to grow from one fertilized egg, and to repair and replace tissues.
  2. Every division has two jobs: replicate the DNA, then segregate the copies into two daughter cells.
  3. Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea): no nucleus, one circular chromosome, often plasmids. Eukaryotes: several linear chromosomes in a nucleus.
  4. Binary fission: prokaryotes → 2 identical cells. Mitosis: eukaryote body cells → 2 identical cells. Meiosis (next module): germ cells → 4 different gametes.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 2

Eukaryotic chromosomes and the cell cycle

THE QUESTION What is a eukaryotic chromosome, and what happens to it before a cell divides?

In this part: one chromosome and its partner (genes, loci, alleles), interphase (G1, S, G2), condensation, counting chromosomes and the DNA molecules in them, and sister chromatids vs. homologs.

START WITH ONE

One chromosome, then its partner: a homologous pair

Before looking at all 46, look at one. Follow one chromosome, then meet its partner from your other parent. That pair is the pattern every other chromosome follows.

INTERACTIVE · 4 STEPS · CHROMOSOME 7

One chromosome, then a pair

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
ONE CHROMOSOMEOne long DNA moleculeA chromosome is one long DNA molecule, wrapped and packed with proteins. This is chromosome 7, the one you got from your mother. The pinch is its centromere.
ITS GENESEach at its own locusAlong that DNA sit many genes, each at a fixed position: its locus. Three are marked here, called A, B and D.
ITS PARTNERChromosome 7 from your fatherYou also got a chromosome 7 from your father. It has the same length, the same centromere position, and the same genes at the same loci.
THE PAIRA homologous pairTogether they are a homologous pair (homologs). Same genes, but each parent's version, its allele, can differ (A from mom, a from dad) or match (B and B).You have 23 pairs like this, one of each pair from each parent. The whole set, the karyotype, comes in Part 3.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Homologous chromosome

One of a pair of chromosomes that carry the same set of genes, one inherited from the mother and one from the father. Their DNA is nearly identical, so their alleles can differ.

Locus

A gene's position (address) on a chromosome; plural loci. Both homologs carry the same gene at the same locus, though the alleles there can differ.

Allele

One version of a gene. Different alleles have slightly different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of every gene, one on each homologous chromosome.

THE WHOLE JOURNEY, ONE STEP AT A TIME

The life cycle: interphase, mitosis, then meiosis

Before zooming into each stage, walk the whole journey once with one pair of chromosomes: from fertilization, through interphase and mitosis (which build a body), to a germ cell's interphase, meiosis I and meiosis II (which make gametes), and on to the next generation. The counter under each step shows exactly when the numbers change.

INTERACTIVE · 19 STEPS · ONE CHROMOSOME PAIR

From fertilization to the next generation

Use Next to walk through all 19 steps
1 · FERTILIZATIONStart: one egg + one spermAn egg (one set of chromosomes, n) fuses with a sperm (one set, n). The new cell, the zygote, has two sets (2n): pink with allele A from the mother, blue with allele a from the father.The two sit side by side as a homologous pair. They never fuse into one chromosome. We follow just this one pair all the way round.
2 · INTERPHASE · G1Interphase is its own stageInterphase is not part of mitosis or meiosis. It is the time between divisions, when the cell lives and works: G1, then S, then G2.In G1 the DNA is loose, still wrapped on its proteins, so the cell can read its genes. 2 chromosomes = 2 DNA molecules.
3 · INTERPHASE · SCopied while looseS phase: each chromosome is copied into two identical sister chromatids held at the centromere. The DNA is still loose: copying needs it open.Count centromeres: still 2 chromosomes. Count chromatids: now 4 DNA molecules. Sisters match (A A, a a).
4 · INTERPHASE · G2Ready to divideStill loose, already copied. The cell grows and gets ready. Interphase ends here, and the division begins.
5 · MITOSIS · PROPHASEWinds up tightOnly now does the DNA wind up tight into compact chromosomes, so they can be moved without tangling.In mitosis each chromosome acts on its own: partners never pair up and nothing is swapped.
6 · MITOSIS · METAPHASESingle fileThe chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell. Each one's sisters are still joined (A with A, a with a).
7 · MITOSIS · ANAPHASESisters pulled apartThe sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends. Each side gets one A and one a. Once apart, each chromatid counts as a chromosome of its own (that is the 4).
8 · MITOSIS · TELOPHASE2 identical cells, not gametesA nucleus forms around each set, the DNA loosens again, and cytokinesis splits the cell.Result of mitosis: 2 identical body cells, each Aa and 2n. Mitosis never makes gametes. Each new cell starts again at G1.
9 · GROWSteps 2 to 8, millions of timesInterphase then mitosis, over and over, builds the whole body. Every cell has the same pair. Most stay body cells forever and never do meiosis.A few, in the ovaries or testes, are germ cells (gold). They are 2n, made by mitosis too, and can do more mitosis. Only they will ever do meiosis.
10 · GERM CELL · INTERPHASEOne copy for all of meiosisWe follow one germ cell (not a gamete). It goes through G1, S and G2 exactly as before, DNA loose the whole time.This S phase is the only copying for the whole of meiosis. There is none between meiosis I and meiosis II.
11 · MEIOSIS I · PROPHASE IPartners pair and cross overMeiosis I begins at prophase I. The DNA winds up tight, and the two partners (homologs) pair up side by side, the only time they ever pair.A pink and a blue chromatid swap pieces where they cross (the gold ring): crossing over. It happens between partners, never between sisters.
12 · MEIOSIS I · METAPHASE IPairs line up togetherThe pairs line up together in the middle, partners on opposite sides. Which partner faces which side is random for every pair: that is independent assortment.
13 · MEIOSIS I · ANAPHASE IPartners pulled apartThe partners are pulled apart: pink one way, blue the other. The sisters stay joined. This is segregation, and the step that halves the chromosome number.
14 · MEIOSIS I · TELOPHASE I2 cells, each n, still doubledThe cell splits into 2. Each has one chromosome of this type, so each is haploid (n), even though that chromosome is still two chromatids: ploidy counts chromosomes (centromeres), not DNA molecules.These are not gametes. The DNA only loosens slightly, and no S phase comes next.
15 · MEIOSIS II · PROPHASE IIBoth cells, no copyingProphase II happens in both cells at once. The chromosomes tighten fully again. Meiosis II works like mitosis, but starts from haploid cells and without copying first.
16 · MEIOSIS II · METAPHASE IISingle file againIn each cell the chromosome lines up single file, sisters on opposite sides, as in mitosis.
17 · MEIOSIS II · ANAPHASE IISisters pulled apartThe sisters are pulled apart in both cells. Each separated chromatid now counts as a chromosome of its own.
18 · MEIOSIS II · TELOPHASE II4 gametesThe DNA loosens fully and 4 haploid gametes form, all different: 2 unmixed, 2 mixed by crossing over. One person makes only eggs or only sperm (a pea flower makes both).Gametes are the end of the line: they never divide again.
19 · FERTILIZATION · NEXT GENERATIONBack to the startAfter meiosis II is finished, one gamete meets one from a different person: 1 + 1 = 1 zygote. That zygote is the next generation, and it starts again at step 1.
NOT DIVIDINGDNA looseEvery interphase (G1, S, G2), and gametes. Copying happens here, in S.
DIVIDINGDNA tightFrom prophase to telophase, in mitosis, meiosis I and meiosis II.
COMMON MIX-UPInterphase is not part of mitosis or meiosis. It is its own stage, between divisions. Mitosis starts at prophase; meiosis I starts at prophase I.
COMMON MIX-UPMitosis never makes gametes. It makes 2 identical body cells. Gametes only come from germ cells, at the end of meiosis II.
COMMON MIX-UPThe end of meiosis I is not gametes. It is 2 cells, each n but still doubled. Meiosis II follows right away, with no S phase.
COMMON MIX-UPFertilization comes after meiosis II, and uses a gamete from a different person. A person's own gametes never fertilize each other (in people; a pea flower can self-fertilize).
GETTING READY

Interphase: grow, copy, get ready (G1, S, G2)

Before a eukaryotic body cell divides by mitosis, it spends most of its life in interphase, getting ready. Interphase has three stages: G1 (grow), S (copy the DNA) and G2 (get ready). The dividing itself, mitosis, comes in Part 3.

INTERACTIVE · 3 STAGES · ONE CELL

Interphase in one cell

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
G1 · GAP 1GrowThe cell grows, makes proteins and does its normal job. Each chromosome is unreplicated: one DNA molecule. This cell has 4: a long pair (A from mom, a from dad) and a short pair (B and B).
S · DNA SYNTHESISCopy every chromosomeEach chromosome's DNA is copied. The copy stays attached at the centromere, so each chromosome is now two sister chromatids.Still 4 chromosomes, but now 8 DNA molecules. (In a real cell the DNA stays unspooled the whole time; it's drawn short so you can follow it.)
G2 · GAP 2Get readyThe cell grows a little more and builds what it needs to divide. Every chromosome is two identical sisters: A and A, a and a, B and B.Next, the cell divides by mitosis (Part 3).
WHICH DIVISION IS THIS FOR?Here: mitosis, in a body cell. Every division of a eukaryotic cell starts with this same interphase, including meiosis later on (Module 3.2), but for now, think of a body cell getting ready to make two copies of itself.
INTERPHASEG1 + S + G2Grow, copy the DNA, get ready. Most of a cell's life.
M PHASEMitosis + cytokinesisDivide the nucleus, then the cell. That's Part 3.
WHEN DO MUTATIONS HAPPEN?Mostly as copying errors in S phase, by chance. More in Module 3.2.
Check yourself: A cell is in G2. What did each chromosome look like in G1, and what happens next?

In G1 each chromosome was one DNA molecule. S copied it, so in G2 it is two sister chromatids. Next comes mitosis, which pulls the sisters apart so each daughter cell gets one.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Interphase

The part of the cell cycle between one M phase and the next: G1, S and G2. The cell grows, copies its DNA and gets ready to divide.

S-phase

The phase of interphase in which DNA is synthesized: every chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids.

UNSPOOLED FOR READING, CONDENSED FOR MOVING

Chromosome condensation

The DNA in one nucleus is 1 to 2 meters long, far wider than the cell, so it is always packed with proteins to fit. During interphase the cell is using its genes, so the DNA is spread out. Only when the cell is about to divide does each chromosome coil up much tighter, into a compact shape you can see, so it does not tangle as it is pulled apart.

INTERACTIVE · ONE CHROMOSOME, THREE STATES

From thread to package

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
INTERPHASE · BEFORE SA long, open threadThe chromosome is one long DNA molecule, unspooled so the cell can read its genes. Chromosomes are not visible under a microscope now.
INTERPHASE · AFTER SCopied, still openAfter replication there are two identical DNA molecules: gene 1 and an exact copy of gene 1. They are still unspooled.
START OF MITOSISPacked up to moveThe two molecules condense into a compact replicated chromosome: two sister chromatids held together at the centromere. Packed this way, they can be moved without tangling.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Sister chromatids

The two identical DNA molecules of a replicated chromosome. They are made in S phase and held together at the centromere until they separate in mitosis.

Centromere

The constriction that holds the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome together. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.

COUNT IT

Counting chromosomes and the DNA molecules inside them

A chromosome is made of DNA: one DNA molecule (plus proteins) before S phase, two identical ones after. So the two counts can differ. Exam questions turn on this one rule: a replicated chromosome is still one chromosome, made of two DNA molecules.

INTERACTIVE · COUNT BEFORE AND AFTER

Count centromeres, then count chromatids

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
BEFORE S PHASE1 chromosome, 1 DNA moleculeAn unreplicated chromosome: one centromere, one DNA molecule.
AFTER S PHASEStill 1 chromosome, now 2 DNA moleculesReplication doubled the DNA but not the number of chromosomes: there is still one centromere, so it is one chromosome, made of two sister chromatids.
AFTER THE SISTERS SEPARATENow each chromatid is a chromosomeWhen mitosis pulls the sisters apart, each one has its own centromere and counts as a full chromosome.
COMMON MIX-UPThe textbook says a chromosome is one DNA molecule (plus proteins). That is true of an unreplicated chromosome, in G1. After S phase the same chromosome is two identical DNA molecules, the sister chromatids, held at one centromere, and it still counts as one chromosome. The book says this too: at the start of mitosis a human cell has 46 chromosomes, each a pair of sister chromatids. And one DNA molecule is itself two strands: strand → molecule → chromosome.
THE RULEChromosomes = centromeres. DNA molecules = chromatids. A replicated chromosome has 2 sister chromatids, so 2 DNA molecules.
Try it on this cell in metaphase.
Check yourself: How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules does the cell above show?

3 chromosomes and 6 DNA molecules. Count the centromeres: 3. Each chromosome is two sister chromatids, so 3 × 2 = 6 DNA molecules.

Check yourself: An unreplicated linear chromosome goes through S phase. How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules come out?

1 chromosome, 2 DNA molecules. It is now two sister chromatids held together at one centromere.

Check yourself: In a stick drawing of a replicated chromosome (two parallel lines joined by one dot), what is each line?

One double-stranded DNA molecule: a sister chromatid. The two are identical in sequence (barring new mutations). Each line is not a single strand, and the two lines are not homologous chromosomes: homologs each have their own centromere.

Check yourself: Which of these is ONE chromosome: a single rod; an X; two parallel rods joined at one centromere; a long double helix with one centromere; two side-by-side replicated chromosomes, each with its own centromere?

The first four. Unreplicated or replicated, straight or X-shaped, one centromere means one chromosome. The last picture has two centromeres: two chromosomes (a homologous pair).

SISTERS VS. HOMOLOGS

Sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, genes and alleles

Most of your cells have two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Keep three ideas apart: sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, and alleles.

INTERACTIVE · TWO PAIRS AFTER S PHASE

Same allele or different?

Tap a button to explore
SISTER CHROMATIDSAlways the same alleleSister chromatids are copies made by replication in S phase, so they carry the same allele of every gene: A and A. That is true for every pair of sisters, unless a new mutation happened.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESA pair, one from each parentTwo chromosomes carrying the same set of genes: one inherited from your mother, one from your father. Their DNA is nearly identical, not identical, so their alleles can differ.
DIFFERENT ALLELES · A AND aSame gene, two versionsThe long pair carries the same gene at the same place, but the mother's version is A and the father's is a. Two different alleles of one gene.
THE SAME ALLELE · B AND BSame gene, same versionThe short pair carries B from the mother and B from the father. The homologs still came from two parents, but here they happen to carry the same allele.
TAP A LABELCopies always match; pairs may notA gene is a stretch of DNA carrying the information for one product. An allele is one version of that gene. Tap each label to see when two alleles are the same and when they differ.
COMMON MIX-UPSister chromatids are copies made in S phase. Homologous chromosomes are a pair you inherited from two parents. Homologs are not copies of each other.
Check yourself: If no mutations have occurred, do two sister chromatids carry the same allele or different alleles of each gene?

The same allele. They were copied from one DNA molecule.

Check yourself: Can you have two different alleles of the same gene in your cells?

Yes. You have one homologous chromosome from each parent, and the two can carry different alleles, such as A from your mother and a from your father.

Check yourself: After S phase but before M phase, how many copies of each gene does a diploid cell have, and how many alleles?

4 copies: two homologs, each made of two sister chromatids. But at most 2 alleles: the sisters carry the same allele, so A, A, a, a is two alleles.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Homologous chromosome

One of a pair of chromosomes that carry the same set of genes, one inherited from the mother and one from the father. Their DNA is nearly identical, so their alleles can differ.

Allele

One version of a gene. Different alleles have slightly different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of every gene, one on each homologous chromosome.

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. The cell cycle: G1 → S → G2 → M (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, cytokinesis). Interphase = G1 + S + G2.
  2. G1: grow. S: replicate every chromosome. G2: get ready. M: mitosis, then cytokinesis.
  3. In interphase chromosomes are unspooled and not visible. They condense at the start of mitosis.
  4. S phase: one chromosome stays one chromosome but goes from 1 to 2 DNA molecules: two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
  5. Count centromeres for chromosomes, chromatids for DNA molecules.
  6. Mutations happen by chance, mostly as copying errors in S phase.
  7. A chromosome is one DNA molecule with many genes, each at its own locus. Its homolog, from the other parent, has the same genes at the same loci; the alleles can differ.
  8. Sister chromatids are identical copies made in S phase (same allele). Homologous chromosomes are a pair from mother and father.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 3

Mitosis, ploidy and the karyotype

THE QUESTION How does mitosis share the copies, and how can you tell what kind of cell you are looking at?

In this part: the mitosis drawings, haploid vs. diploid cells, the human karyotype, chromosome numbers across species, and where mitosis fits in a life cycle. (Gametes, fertilization and meiosis are in the next module.)

M PHASE

Mitosis: the drawings to know

Exam questions ask you to draw the same cell at a few moments: before DNA replication, after it, at metaphase, at anaphase, and as the two daughter cells. Here is that set for the cell from the cell cycle step, with every chromosome drawn as what it really is: DNA. Follow the molecules: one per chromosome in G1, two per chromosome after S, and one per chromosome again in each daughter cell. Prophase and telophase are left out here; to see every stage, tap through the complete cycle in Part 2.

INTERACTIVE · ONE CELL, EVERY DNA MOLECULE

From one cell to two, molecule by molecule

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
INTERPHASE · G1Each chromosome is one DNA moleculeEvery chromosome is one double-stranded DNA molecule: two strands twisted around each other. This cell has 4: a long pair (A from the mother, a from the father) and a short pair (B and B).4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules. In the real cell each one is a long, loose thread; they are drawn short so you can see the two strands.
INTERPHASE · SDNA replication: one molecule becomes twoZoom in on chromosome A. Its two strands come apart, and each one is the template for a new partner strand (dashed).The result is two DNA molecules, each one original strand and one new strand, held together at the centromere. They are the two sister chromatids, and both carry allele A: two copies of the same allele.In the real cell the strands come apart a little at a time, at many spots at once, and the new strand is built right behind the opening. The drawing splits it into two moments so you can see it.
INTERPHASE · G2Every chromosome is now two moleculesAll 4 chromosomes were copied the same way. Each is now two sister chromatids joined at one centromere: A and A, a and a, B and B, B and B.Still 4 chromosomes (count the centromeres), but 8 DNA molecules (count the chromatids).
M PHASE · METAPHASELine up in the middleProphase has coiled each chromosome up (shorter here). Now each replicated chromosome lines up separately in the middle of the cell, with spindle fibers from both poles attached at its centromere, so one sister faces each pole.Still 4 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules.
M PHASE · ANAPHASEThe two molecules separateThe centromeres split and the spindle pulls the two DNA molecules of every chromosome to opposite poles. Each molecule is now its own chromosome.For a moment the cell holds 8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules: A, a, B and B on each side.
AFTER TELOPHASE + CYTOKINESISTwo daughter cells, identical to the parentTelophase builds a nucleus around each set, and cytokinesis splits the cell in two. Each daughter has 4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules, alleles A a B B: exactly what the parent had in G1.Each molecule is one original strand and one new strand, but the sequence is the same, so the copies are identical. Each daughter starts again in G1.
WHAT TO TRACKJust three moments. After S: each chromosome is two sisters. Metaphase: they line up separately. Anaphase: the sisters separate, one copy to each side.
GO DEEPERThe textbook gives the end of prophase its own name, prometaphase: the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle attaches at the centromeres.
