STEP THROUGH IT · ONE COLOR PER CHROMOSOME

Mitosis keeps the number

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
PROPHASE5 chromosomes, 10 DNA moleculesEach chromosome was copied in S phase, so each is two identical sister chromatids. One color per chromosome makes each one easy to follow.
METAPHASESingle fileEach replicated chromosome lines up on its own in the middle. Sisters are still joined, so the count hasn't changed.
ANAPHASEEvery pair of sisters splitsOne copy of every color goes to each pole. For a moment the cell holds 10 chromosomes.
TWO DAUGHTERSOne of each color: 5 againEach daughter gets one copy of all 5 chromosomes. Mitosis undoes the copying; it never halves the number.
COMMON MIX-UPMitosis never swaps pieces. The two sisters are identical copies, and the point of copying is a full set for each new cell. Swapping happens only in meiosis I (crossing over), between partner chromosomes, never sisters: see Module 3.2.
M MEANS MITOSISThe M in M phase is named for mitosis. Meiosis is a separate division that only germ cells do.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
M-phase

The part of the cell cycle in which the cell divides: mitosis followed by cytokinesis.

Cytokinesis

Division of the cytoplasm, which splits one cell into two daughter cells. It follows mitosis.

Check yourself: A cell with 5 replicated chromosomes in G2 goes through mitosis. How many chromosomes are in the nucleus of each daughter cell?

5. Each of the 5 is split into its two sister chromatids, and one of each goes to each daughter. Mitosis keeps the number the same.

Check yourself: Is the parent cell in these drawings haploid or diploid, and how can you tell from the metaphase drawing?

Diploid (2n = 4). At metaphase there are two long and two short chromosomes: two homologous pairs.

Check yourself: Somatic cells of scarlet dragonflies are diploid with 50 chromosomes. A skin cell divides by mitosis. How many chromatids are in the cell at prophase? At metaphase? How many chromosomes in each daughter cell?

100, 100, 50. After S phase each of the 50 chromosomes is two sister chromatids: 100 chromatids at prophase and still 100 at metaphase. Anaphase splits the sisters, so each daughter gets 50 chromosomes, like the parent.

ONE SET OR TWO?

Haploid vs. diploid cells

Haploid and diploid are about how many sets of chromosomes a cell has. A set is one of every type. Gametes (eggs and sperm) have one set: haploid, n. Somatic cells (every other body cell) have two sets, one from each parent: diploid, 2n. That's true whether the chromosomes are unreplicated or replicated: the question is whether each type has a separate partner. Sister chromatids don't count as a second set, because they are the same chromosome copied.

INTERACTIVE · 4 STEPS · ONE SET OR TWO

Gametes vs. somatic cells, replicated or not

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
HAPLOID · ONE SETA gameteAn egg or sperm holds one complete set: one chromosome of each type, every one different in length, centromere position and bands. In this sketch n = 4; in humans n = 23.
DIPLOID · TWO SETSA somatic cellA somatic cell has the same types, but each type has a separate matching partner: one set from the mother (pink), one from the father (blue). 2n = 8 here, 46 in humans.
REPLICATED · STILL HAPLOIDCopies aren't partnersAfter replication each chromosome is two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. There is still only one chromosome of each type, so the cell is still haploid. Sister chromatids are the same chromosome copied.
REPLICATED · STILL DIPLOIDCount separate chromosomesA somatic cell after S phase still has two separate chromosomes of each type, each now two sisters. Still diploid. The quick test: pick one type and count the centromeres. One → haploid. Two → diploid.
INTERACTIVE · ONE SET OR TWO, STEP BY STEP

Think of the chromosomes as a set of books

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
HAPLOID · ONE SET (n)One copy of each kind of chromosomePicture the chromosomes as a set of instruction books: book 1, book 2, book 3, each with different genes. A haploid cell has one complete set: one copy of each book.n is the number of different kinds of chromosomes in one set. This egg has n = 3. In humans, n = 23.
DIPLOID · TWO SETS (2n)Two copies of each kind, one from each parentA diploid cell has two complete sets: one set came from the mother's egg (pink), the other from the father's sperm (blue). So every kind of chromosome is there twice.The two copies of one kind are a homologous pair. This cell is 2n = 6: three pairs. Your body cells are 2n = 46: 23 pairs.
HOMOLOGS · SAME BOOK, TWO EDITIONSSame genes, maybe different allelesThe two homologs carry the same genes in the same places, like two editions of one book with the same chapters. The wording of a chapter can differ: those versions are alleles (A from mom, a from dad).So a diploid cell has two alleles of every gene (they may match or differ), and a haploid cell has one.
THE TRAP · COPYING DOESN'T ADD A SETA photocopy isn't a second editionIn S phase each chromosome is copied, and the copy stays stuck to it as a sister chromatid, like photocopying book 1 and clipping the copy to the original. You still have only book 1 from one parent: no new type, no edition from the other parent.A second set means a second chromosome of every type from the other parent, and that only comes from fertilization. So copying never changes ploidy: this haploid cell is still haploid (n = 3) after S.
IN HUMANS23 or 46Egg: n = 23. Sperm: n = 23. Fertilization: n + n = 2n = 46, the zygote. Mitosis then copies those 46 into every body cell.Only the gametes are haploid. They are made by meiosis, which halves 46 to 23 (Module 3.2).
HAPLOIDDIPLOID
Sets of chromosomes12, one from each parent
Written asn2n
Copies of each kind12: a homologous pair
Alleles of each gene12 (same or different)
In humans23 chromosomes46 chromosomes
Which cellsGametes: eggs and spermSomatic (body) cells, the zygote
COMMON MIX-UPDiploid does not mean "replicated". Two sister chromatids are copies of one chromosome. Diploid means each kind of chromosome is there twice as two different homologs, one from each parent.
REMEMBER IT BY THE WORDDi-ploid: di = two, -ploid = -fold, so two sets (not two chromosomes): every kind of chromosome twice, as homologous pairs. Hap-loid: from Greek haplous, single, so one set: one of each kind, no pairs, every chromosome different (non-homologous).
THE QUICK TESTPick one kind of chromosome (say the longest) and count how many there are, counting a pair of sister chromatids as one. One → haploid. Two → diploid. Then n = how many different kinds there are.
GO DEEPER · FROM THE TEXTBOOKThe number of complete sets in a cell is its ploidy. Some organisms, especially plants, have four sets (4n) or more: they are polyploid.
PRACTICE · SORT FIVE CELLS

Haploid or diploid?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
CELL 1 · HAPLOID, n = 3No pairsThree chromosomes, every one different. One set, so haploid.
CELL 2 · DIPLOID, 2n = 6Three pairsEach chromosome has a match of the same length and genes: three homologous pairs, two sets. Diploid.
CELL 3 · HAPLOID, n = 2Replicated, but still no pairsTwo replicated chromosomes that are different from each other. Being replicated does not make a cell diploid: the two sisters are copies, not a pair. Haploid.
CELL 4 · HAPLOID, n = 3Read the genesIn metaphase the chromosomes carry genes g, e and f. Each gene appears on only one chromosome (twice, on its two sisters), so there are no homologous pairs. Haploid.
CELL 5 · CAN'T TELLTwo chromosomes, no labelsFrom the number alone, you can't tell. If the two are homologs carrying the same genes, it is diploid (2n = 2). If they carry different genes, it is haploid (n = 2).
HOW TO TELLCount pairs, not chromosomes. Matching chromosomes with the same genes means diploid. All different means haploid.
Check yourself: Can a haploid cell go through mitosis? Can a diploid cell?

Yes, both. Mitosis copies whatever chromosomes a cell has and gives each daughter the same set. A haploid cell makes haploid daughters, and a diploid cell makes diploid daughters.

Check yourself: Are your somatic cells haploid or diploid?

Diploid. Your somatic cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Only your gametes, eggs or sperm, are haploid.

Check yourself: A cell has 8 chromosomes: 4 kinds, two of each. What are n and 2n, and is it haploid or diploid?

n = 4, 2n = 8, diploid. Two copies of each of 4 kinds means two sets. A gamete from this organism would have 4 chromosomes, one of each kind.

Check yourself: A cell has two replicated chromosomes: one carries A on both sister chromatids, the other carries b on both. Haploid or diploid? Replicated or not?

Haploid, replicated. Each chromosome is two sisters (A A, b b), and the two chromosomes carry different genes, so there are no pairs: one set.

Check yourself: A cell has two unreplicated chromosomes side by side, one with allele A and one with allele a at the same place. Haploid or diploid? Replicated or not?

Diploid, unreplicated. A and a are alleles of the same gene at the same place, so the two are homologs: a pair, two sets. Each is a single molecule, so not replicated.

FROM CLASS · PAIRS OF SHOESIn class, homologous chromosomes were compared to pairs of shoes: two of the same kind (same genes), which can differ in style (alleles). A diploid cell has a closet of pairs; a haploid cell has one shoe of each kind. And a haploid cell is not always small: a cell with four different chromosomes is haploid, n = 4.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Haploid

A cell with one complete set of chromosomes (n). Every chromosome carries a different set of genes, so there are no homologous pairs.

Diploid

A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes (2n), so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. Most human cells are diploid.

YOUR CHROMOSOMES

The karyotype: 46 chromosomes, 23 types

Now the whole human set. Most human cells have 46 chromosomes, but they aren't 46 of the same thing: they are 23 different types, two of each. Biologists tell the types apart by three things: size, where the centromere sits, and their pattern of stained bands.

INTERACTIVE · 8 STEPS · A HUMAN KARYOTYPE

From a messy spread to 23 pairs

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 8
UNDER THE MICROSCOPENot neat X'sStop a cell in mitosis, squash it flat and stain it, and this is what you see: 46 bent, fuzzy, overlapping shapes. Diagrams draw tidy X's; real chromosomes look wonky.They're replicated at this point: each is two sister chromatids held tight at the centromere, which is why diagrams draw them as X's. See a real one: the National Human Genome Research Institute's karyotype.
THE KARYOTYPESorted into pairsPhotograph the chromosomes, then line them up in pairs: that's a karyotype, the textbook's "portrait formed by the number and shapes of chromosomes." 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs.The two chromosomes of a pair are homologous chromosomes (homologs). A karyotype is one picture of a cell's whole set; a homologous pair is two chromosomes inside it.
SIZENumbered longest to shortest (almost)The 22 numbered pairs go from the longest (chromosome 1) down to the shortest.One surprise: when they were named, 22 looked like the smallest, but 21 is actually a little shorter than 22. So it's "roughly" by size.
CENTROMERE POSITIONWhere the pinch isThe centromere sits in a fixed spot for each type: near the middle (chromosome 1), off-center (4) or near one end (13). Same length can still mean different types.
BANDSA barcode for each typeA stain gives every type its own pattern of dark and light bands. Both members of a pair have the same length, centromere and bands: that's how the pairs are matched.
AUTOSOMES22 types, 22 sets of genesPairs 1 to 22 are the autosomes. Each type carries a different set of genes; that's why the types aren't interchangeable.
SEX CHROMOSOMESThe 23rd pair: X and YThe 23rd pair are the sex chromosomes: XX in genetic females, XY in genetic males (this karyotype is male).X and Y are the important exception: a different size and different genes, so they are a pair that doesn't match. Every other pair matches.
LOCUSA gene's addressA locus (Latin for place; plural loci) is a gene's position on a chromosome. Same word as "locus of control" in psychology, where you feel control is located; here it's where a gene is located.Both homologs have the same gene at the same locus. The version sitting at that address, the allele, can differ: A on one, a on the other.
FROM A FAMOUS PAPERUntil 1956, textbooks said humans had 48 chromosomes. Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan, with better ways to spread the chromosomes out, counted 46: "The chromosome number of man," Hereditas 42:1–6 (1956), doi:10.1111/j.1601-5223.1956.tb03010.x.
COMMON MIX-UPThe "two of each type" are homologs: two different chromosomes, one from each parent. Sister chromatids are something else: the two copies a chromosome makes of itself in S phase.
OTHER SPECIESEvery species has its own number: horse cells have 64 chromosomes, corn has 20.
Check yourself: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes. How many types? How many of each? Which pair breaks the pattern?

23 types, 2 of each (one from each parent). The sex chromosomes break the pattern in males: X and Y are a pair but differ in size and genes.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Karyotype

The portrait of a species' chromosomes: a picture of one cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs and numbered. Humans: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.

Autosomes

Chromosomes 1 to 22 in humans: every chromosome except the sex chromosomes. Each type carries a different set of genes.

Sex chromosomes

The 23rd pair in humans, X and Y: XX in genetic females, XY in genetic males. X and Y differ in size and genes, the exception to matching pairs.

Locus

A gene's position (address) on a chromosome; plural loci. Both homologs carry the same gene at the same locus, though the alleles there can differ.

Homologous chromosome

One of a pair of chromosomes that carry the same set of genes, one inherited from the mother and one from the father. Their DNA is nearly identical, so their alleles can differ.

Centromere

The constriction that holds the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome together. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.

NOT THE SAME FOR EVERY SPECIES

Chromosome numbers across species

Humans have 46, but the number isn't a rule of life: every species has its own. What stays the same is the pattern: body cells have 2n (two sets), gametes have n (one set). Click through.

INTERACTIVE · 8 SPECIES · 2n AND n

Same pattern, different numbers

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 8
FRUIT FLY · 2n = 8, n = 4Fruit flyBody cells: 8 chromosomes in 4 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 4, one of each type. Drosophila melanogaster: the fly geneticists use.
GARDEN PEA · 2n = 14, n = 7Garden peaBody cells: 14 chromosomes in 7 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 7, one of each type. Pisum sativum: Mendel's plant.
CORN · 2n = 20, n = 10CornBody cells: 20 chromosomes in 10 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 10, one of each type. Zea mays.
CAT · 2n = 38, n = 19CatBody cells: 38 chromosomes in 19 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 19, one of each type. Felis catus.
HUMAN · 2n = 46, n = 23HumanBody cells: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 23, one of each type. Homo sapiens.
CHIMPANZEE · 2n = 48, n = 24ChimpanzeeBody cells: 48 chromosomes in 24 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 24, one of each type. Pan troglodytes: two more than us.
HORSE · 2n = 64, n = 32HorseBody cells: 64 chromosomes in 32 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 32, one of each type. Equus caballus.
DOG · 2n = 78, n = 39DogBody cells: 78 chromosomes in 39 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 39, one of each type. Canis familiaris: more than a human.
NUMBER ISN'T COMPLEXITYA dog (78) has more chromosomes than a human (46), and a chimpanzee has two more than we do. One ant species, Myrmecia pilosula, has just 2n = 2: a single pair. The count says how the DNA is packaged, not how complex the organism is.
Check yourself: A horse body cell has 64 chromosomes. What are 2n and n, and how many chromosomes are in a horse sperm?

2n = 64, n = 32. A sperm is a gamete, so it has one set: 32.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Haploid

A cell with one complete set of chromosomes (n). Every chromosome carries a different set of genes, so there are no homologous pairs.

Diploid

A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes (2n), so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. Most human cells are diploid.

THE BIG PICTURE

Mitosis in a life cycle (and where meiosis fits)

Mitosis and meiosis are two separate processes with two different jobs, happening at different points in a life. Mitosis copies cells (2n → 2n) to build and repair your body, all your life. Meiosis halves the number (2n → n), only in germ cells, only to make eggs and sperm for the next generation. Follow the loop from the start.

INTERACTIVE · 5 STEPS · THE HUMAN LIFE CYCLE

A loop with a start: where mitosis and meiosis each happen

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
START HERE · THE ZYGOTEYou began as one cellEvery person starts as one cell, the zygote: diploid (2n), with one set of chromosomes from mom's egg and one from dad's sperm.
MITOSIS · ALL YOUR LIFECopy, then share, again and againThe zygote divides by mitosis, and so do its daughters, again and again: that's how you grow and how you repair. Every cell made this way is 2n with the same DNA. This is the division this module is about.
GERM CELLSA few cells set asideMost of your cells are somatic (skin, gut, blood). A few are germ cells, kept in the gonads (ovaries or testes). They're 2n too, and mitosis made them like every other cell.
MEIOSIS · ONLY HEREGerm cells make gametesMeiosis is a different division with a different job: it happens only in germ cells, and only to make gametes (eggs or sperm). It halves the number: 2n → n. That's Module 3.2.
FERTILIZATIONBack to the startAn egg (n) and a sperm (n) fuse: n + n = 2n, a new zygote, the start of the next generation. The loop begins again.
SCENE · DIFFERENT CELLS, SAME DNA

Does a skin cell have different DNA from a liver cell?

No. Every somatic cell came from the same zygote by mitosis, so they all have the same DNA, except for any new mutations. Cells differ in which genes they use, not in which genes they have.
ANIMALS VS. PLANTS AND FUNGIMeiosis makes gametes directly only in animals. In plants and fungi, meiosis makes haploid spores, which divide by mitosis into the cells that make gametes (in seed plants, pollen makes the sperm). More in Module 3.2.
COMMON MIX-UPGerm cells are not gametes. Germ cells are diploid cells in the ovaries or testes; they undergo meiosis to make the haploid gametes (eggs and sperm). Germ cells can also divide by mitosis to make more germ cells.
Check yourself: Which of these is NOT accurate? (A) Binary fission happens in bacteria, archaea, mitochondria and chloroplasts. (B) Somatic cells do mitosis but not meiosis. (C) Diploid germ cells do meiosis to make haploid gametes in animals. (D) Diploid germ cells can do mitosis to make more germ cells. (E) Eukaryotes copy their DNA before dividing but bacteria do not. (F) Mitosis can happen in haploid or diploid cells. (G) Meiosis only happens in diploid germ cells. (H) Germ cells are the same as gametes.

E and H are inaccurate. Bacteria do copy their DNA before binary fission (every division copies first). And germ cells make gametes by meiosis; they are not gametes themselves. A is true because mitochondria and chloroplasts came from bacteria (endosymbiosis, Module 2.2).

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Somatic cells

The cells of the body other than the cells that make gametes. Human somatic cells are diploid and are made by mitosis.

Gametes

Haploid reproductive cells: eggs and sperm. They are made by meiosis, and two of them fuse at fertilization.

Sexual reproduction

Reproduction in which two haploid gametes fuse at fertilization, so the offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase, then cytokinesis. Each daughter gets the same DNA and alleles.
  2. Haploid (n): one set, the gametes. Diploid (2n): two sets, the somatic cells. Replicated or not; sister chromatids are not a second set.
  3. A karyotype: a cell's chromosomes sorted into pairs. Humans: 46 chromosomes, 23 types (22 autosome pairs + the sex chromosomes), told apart by size, centromere position and bands.
  4. Chromosome numbers differ by species (fruit fly 2n = 8, human 46, dog 78), but body cells are 2n and gametes n.
  5. Every somatic cell has the same DNA; cells differ in which genes they use.
Vocab · 26 terms
Unicellular Made of a single cell. For a unicellular organism, cell division is reproduction.
Multicellular Made of many cells, like animals, plants and most fungi. Only eukaryotes are multicellular. Cell division builds and repairs the body; reproduction is a separate job.
Mitosis Division of the nucleus in which the sister chromatids of every chromosome are pulled apart, so each daughter cell gets the same DNA as the parent cell.
Meiosis The cell division that turns a diploid cell into four haploid gametes, whose DNA is different from the parent cell's.
Plasmid A small circle of DNA in a prokaryotic cell, separate from the chromosome. It usually carries genes that are not essential for the species.
Chromosome One double-stranded DNA molecule packaged with proteins. It carries many genes. After S phase it is two sister chromatids, but it still counts as one chromosome.
Nuclear DNA The DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, organized into linear chromosomes. In eukaryotes, "genome" usually means the nuclear DNA.
Conjugation A way prokaryotes share DNA: one cell passes a copy of some of its DNA, often a plasmid, to another cell through a connecting bridge. No new cell is made, so it is not reproduction.
Asexual reproduction Reproduction by one parent alone, by mitosis (or binary fission in prokaryotes). The offspring have the same DNA as the parent, except new mutations.
Interphase The part of the cell cycle between one M phase and the next: G1, S and G2. The cell grows, copies its DNA and gets ready to divide.
S-phase The phase of interphase in which DNA is synthesized: every chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids.
M-phase The part of the cell cycle in which the cell divides: mitosis followed by cytokinesis.
Cytokinesis Division of the cytoplasm, which splits one cell into two daughter cells. It follows mitosis.
Sister chromatids The two identical DNA molecules of a replicated chromosome. They are made in S phase and held together at the centromere until they separate in mitosis.
Centromere The constriction that holds the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome together. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.
Karyotype The portrait of a species' chromosomes: a picture of one cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs and numbered. Humans: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
Autosomes Chromosomes 1 to 22 in humans: every chromosome except the sex chromosomes. Each type carries a different set of genes.
Sex chromosomes The 23rd pair in humans, X and Y: XX in genetic females, XY in genetic males. X and Y differ in size and genes, the exception to matching pairs.
Locus A gene's position (address) on a chromosome; plural loci. Both homologs carry the same gene at the same locus, though the alleles there can differ.
Homologous chromosome One of a pair of chromosomes that carry the same set of genes, one inherited from the mother and one from the father. Their DNA is nearly identical, so their alleles can differ.
Allele One version of a gene. Different alleles have slightly different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of every gene, one on each homologous chromosome.
Haploid A cell with one complete set of chromosomes (n). Every chromosome carries a different set of genes, so there are no homologous pairs.
Diploid A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes (2n), so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. Most human cells are diploid.
Gametes Haploid reproductive cells: eggs and sperm. They are made by meiosis, and two of them fuse at fertilization.
Somatic cells The cells of the body other than the cells that make gametes. Human somatic cells are diploid and are made by mitosis.
Sexual reproduction Reproduction in which two haploid gametes fuse at fertilization, so the offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

Notes

Everything you are expected to know for this module, in the order the learning objectives ask for it. Read it once, then use the checklist at the end.

IN THESE NOTES1 · How genetic material is arranged2 · What mitosis and binary fission are for3 · Who divides how4 · Genes and alleles5 · The eukaryotic cell cycle6 · Mitosis, drawn out7 · Haploid and diploid8 · Reading a karyotype9 · Large numbers of chromosomes10 · Cell division in a life cycle11 · Exam checklist
THE BIG IDEA

Every cell division copies the DNA, then shares it out. Bacteria do it by binary fission. Eukaryotes copy every chromosome in S phase and split the sister chromatids in mitosis, so each daughter cell gets the same DNA as the parent. Diploid cells carry chromosomes in homologous pairs, one from each parent.

SECTION 1OBJECTIVE 10

How genetic material is arranged

PROKARYOTESEUKARYOTES
DomainsBacteria, ArchaeaEukarya (unicellular or multicellular)
NucleusNoneYes, plus other compartments
ChromosomesOne circular chromosomeUsually more than one linear chromosome
Extra DNAPlasmids: small, usually non-essential genesCircular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts
How they divideBinary fissionMitosis (somatic cells); meiosis (germ cells only)
  • Each chromosome is one double-stranded DNA molecule packaged with proteins, carrying many genes.
  • In eukaryotes, genome usually means the nuclear DNA.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts have circular DNA because they descend from engulfed bacteria (endosymbiosis, Module 2.2); they still divide by binary fission.
  • Where vs. form vs. stage: prokaryote DNA is in one place (the cytoplasm); eukaryote DNA is in the nucleus (linear) and in mitochondria and chloroplasts (circular). Nucleus → chromosome → DNA → gene are zoom levels, not places. The cell cycle changes the packing (loose threads in interphase, condensed in mitosis), not the place.
SECTION 2OBJECTIVE 6

What mitosis and binary fission are for

  • Why cells divide: reproduction (one-celled organisms, and asexual reproduction in some species), development and growth from a single fertilized egg, and repair and regeneration of tissues.
  • Every division has two parts: replication of the DNA, then segregation of the copies into two daughter cells.
  • Binary fission (bacteria, archaea, and mitochondria and chloroplasts): the circular DNA is attached to the membrane; copying starts at the origin of replication and runs both ways; the copy gets its own attachment site next to the first; the cell grows so the two circles move apart; at about twice its size a ring of FtsZ pinches it in two. It is regulated by nutrient availability.
  • Mitosis (eukaryotes): needed because the DNA is in a nucleus on several linear chromosomes, so the copies must be pulled apart by the spindle.
MITOSISMEIOSIS
Divisions12 in a row: meiosis I (homologous pairs split), meiosis II (sister chromatids split)
Daughter cells24 (gametes)
DNA vs. the parentIdentical (except new mutations)Different
Chromosome numberKept: 2n → 2nHalved: 2n → n
WhereSomatic cellsOnly germ cells
What forGrowth, repair, asexual reproductionSexual reproduction
SECTION 3

Who divides how

  • Three domains: Bacteria and Archaea (prokaryotes, always unicellular) and Eukarya (eukaryotes, unicellular like yeast and amoebas, or multicellular like animals, plants and most fungi). Archaea are the closest relatives of eukaryotes.
  • Prokaryotes: binary fission only, never mitosis or meiosis.
  • Eukaryotes that reproduce sexually: mitosis in somatic cells and meiosis in germ cells, both in the same organism. Reproduction = meiosis + fertilization.
  • Eukaryotes that reproduce asexually: mitosis only, no meiosis (yeast budding, strawberry runners, aphids). Many species do both.
  • Genetically identical copies: binary fission and mitosis. Recombination: conjugation in prokaryotes (DNA passed between cells, not reproduction) and meiosis + fertilization in eukaryotes.
GO DEEPERTheir trade-offs are in Module 3.2.
SECTION 4OBJECTIVE 5

Genes and alleles

  • A locus is a gene's address on a chromosome. Both homologs have the same gene at the same locus; the allele there can differ
  • A gene is a stretch of DNA carrying the information for one product. Each chromosome carries many genes.
  • An allele is one version of a gene. Alleles of the same gene have slightly different DNA sequences.
  • Each chromosome has one allele per gene. A diploid cell has 2 alleles of every gene, one on each homolog. They can be the same or different.
  • After S phase, a diploid cell has 4 copies of each gene but still at most 2 alleles, because sister chromatids carry the same allele.
  • Exception: the X and Y sex chromosomes form a pair but carry different sets of genes.
DIFFERENT ALLELESThe long pair in the example cell: A from the mother, a from the father. Same gene, different versions.
THE SAME ALLELEThe short pair: B from the mother and B from the father. Homologs can match. Sister chromatids always match, because one was copied from the other.
SECTION 5OBJECTIVES 1 AND 2

The eukaryotic cell cycle

  • G1 (gap 1): the cell grows and replicates its organelles. Each chromosome is one DNA molecule.
  • S (DNA synthesis): every chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
  • G2 (gap 2): the cell keeps growing and prepares to divide. Each chromosome is two sister chromatids.
  • M: mitosis (the nucleus divides), then cytokinesis (the cytoplasm divides). Each daughter starts again in G1.
  • Interphase = G1 + S + G2. Checkpoints make sure the cell is ready before it moves on.
  • In interphase, chromosomes are unspooled so genes can be read, and they are not visible under a microscope. They condense at the start of mitosis.
PHASEEACH CHROMOSOME ISDNA MOLECULES PER CHROMOSOME
G1Unreplicated1
SBeing copied1 → 2
G2Replicated: 2 sister chromatids2
M, after anaphaseSeparated: each chromatid is now a chromosome1
COUNTING RULEChromosomes = centromeres. DNA molecules = chromatids. Replication doubles the DNA, not the number of chromosomes.
  • Mutations happen by chance, mostly as copying errors when DNA is replicated in S phase; they can also happen during mitosis.
SECTION 6OBJECTIVE 4

Mitosis, drawn out

  • Start (G1): each chromosome unreplicated. After S: each chromosome is two sister chromatids with the same allele.
  • Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible; the mitotic spindle forms from two poles; the nuclear envelope breaks down (the textbook calls that part prometaphase).
  • Metaphase: each replicated chromosome lines up separately in the middle, attached to spindle fibers from both poles.
  • Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles. Each is now a chromosome.
  • Telophase: a nuclear envelope forms around each set. Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm splits into two daughter cells.
  • Result: two daughter cells with the same chromosomes and alleles as the parent cell.
STAGECELL WITH 2n = 2CHROMOSOMESDNA MOLECULES
G1A and a, unreplicated22
After SA A and a a24
Metaphaselined up separately24
Anaphasesisters pulled apart44
Each daughterA and a22
SISTER CHROMATIDSTwo identical copies made in S phase. Same allele. Held together at the centromere until anaphase.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESA pair, one from the mother and one from the father. Same genes, nearly identical DNA, so alleles can differ.
SECTION 7OBJECTIVE 3

Haploid and diploid

  • Think of books: each kind of chromosome is a different book. A set is one copy of every book. Haploid = one set; diploid = two sets, one edition from each parent. The two editions of one book are a homologous pair: same genes (chapters), maybe different alleles (wording).
  • Copying is not a second set: sister chromatids are photocopies of one chromosome. A haploid cell stays haploid after S phase; ploidy counts sets, not DNA copies.
  • Quick test: count how many of one kind of chromosome there are (a pair of sisters counts as one). One → haploid, two → diploid; n = number of different kinds. Humans: n = 23, 2n = 46. Some plants are polyploid (4n or more).
  • One chromosome = one DNA molecule before S phase; after S it is two molecules (sister chromatids) at one centromere, still one chromosome.
  • Haploid (n): one complete set of chromosomes. Every chromosome carries a different set of genes; there are no pairs.
  • Diploid (2n): two complete sets, so chromosomes come in homologous pairs, one from each parent.
  • How to tell: look for pairs of matching chromosomes (same size, same genes). Replicated sister chromatids are copies, not a pair.
  • A cell with only 2 chromosomes: you can't tell from the number alone. Homologous → diploid (2n = 2). Different genes → haploid (n = 2).
  • Both haploid and diploid cells can go through mitosis. Your somatic cells are diploid; gametes are haploid.
SECTION 8OBJECTIVE 7

Reading a karyotype

  • Humans have 46 chromosomes of 23 types, two of each: 22 pairs of autosomes plus the sex chromosomes (XX or XY). Types are told apart by size, centromere position and stained bands. Numbered roughly longest to shortest (21 is actually a little shorter than 22). Real chromosomes look bent and fuzzy, not like neat X's
  • A karyotype is a picture of all of a cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs. It is made during mitosis, when they are condensed and visible.
  • Human somatic cells: 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs: 22 numbered pairs, longest (1) to shortest (22), plus the sex chromosomes, XX or XY.
  • Two copies of each numbered chromosome means human somatic cells are diploid.
  • Before S phase each chromosome (1) has many genes, (2) has one allele per gene, (3) is a single double-stranded DNA molecule.
SECTION 9OBJECTIVE 8

Large numbers of chromosomes

  • The number differs by species, but the pattern doesn't: fruit fly 2n = 8 (n = 4), pea 14 (7), corn 20 (10), cat 38 (19), human 46 (23), chimpanzee 48 (24), horse 64 (32), dog 78 (39)
  • The logic doesn't change with the number. A horse cell has 64 chromosomes: 64 DNA molecules in G1, 128 after S, and each daughter cell gets 64 after mitosis.
  • A human cell: 46 chromosomes in G1 (46 DNA molecules), 46 chromosomes but 92 DNA molecules in G2, 46 in each daughter.
  • Mitosis never changes the chromosome number: a cell with 5 replicated chromosomes in G2 gives daughters with 5 each.
SECTION 10OBJECTIVE 9

Cell division in a life cycle

  • Humans: a diploid zygote (fertilized egg) divides by mitosis many times to build every somatic cell.
  • Meiosis in germ cells makes haploid gametes (eggs and sperm). At fertilization two gametes fuse into a new diploid zygote: sexual reproduction.
  • Every somatic cell came from the same zygote, so skin, muscle, heart and liver cells all have the same DNA, except new mutations. They differ in which genes they use.
CELLPLOIDYCHROMOSOMES IN THE EXAMPLE
EggHaploid, n = 2long A, short B
SpermHaploid, n = 2long a, short B
Zygote (egg + sperm)Diploid, 2n = 4long pair A and a, short pair B and B
n + n = 2nFertilization is what makes a cell diploid: each homologous pair is one chromosome from the egg and one from the sperm.
SECTION 11

Exam checklist

You're ready when you can:

  • Draw the cell cycle with G1, S, G2 and M, mark interphase, and say what each chromosome looks like in each phase.
  • Given a cell at one stage, say what its chromosomes looked like before and will look like after.
  • Tell a haploid cell from a diploid cell in a drawing, including a replicated cell and a cell with only two chromosomes.
  • Draw mitosis for a cell with two chromosomes, before and after S, at metaphase and in the daughter cells, and point out sister chromatids and homologs.
  • Explain the difference between a gene and an allele, and count alleles and gene copies before and after S.
  • Give at least three reasons cells divide, and describe binary fission and what regulates its speed.
  • Compare mitosis and meiosis: number of cells, DNA, ploidy, where and why.
  • Read a human karyotype: count, pairs and sex chromosomes.
  • Count chromosomes and DNA molecules for any number of chromosomes (64, 46, 20) through the cycle.
  • Place mitosis, meiosis and fertilization in a human life cycle.
  • Show how a haploid egg and a haploid sperm make a diploid zygote, and point out which pairs carry the same allele and which carry different alleles.
  • Compare how DNA is organized in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and explain why mitochondria and chloroplasts have circular DNA.
  • Name the three domains, give unicellular and multicellular examples, and say which kind of division each group uses.
  • Say what meiosis I and meiosis II each separate, and why they are not generations.
  • Compare asexual and sexual reproduction, and tell genotype from phenotype.
COMMON MIX-UPMitosis gives 2 identical daughter cells. Meiosis gives 4 different gametes. And sister chromatids are copies, while homologous chromosomes are a pair from two parents.

Infographics

Every diagram from the flow charts in one place, without the reading in between. Start with the one-page map, then scan the rest.

INFOGRAPHIC 1 · THE WHOLE MODULE ON ONE PAGE
MODULE 3.1 · PART 1

Why cells divide, and binary fission

Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. What are the two jobs of every division, where is the DNA, and how do prokaryotes divide?

1Why do cells divide?
Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. Cell division is how one cell becomes two, and there are several reasons a living thing needs it.
2Replication, then segregation
Whatever the reason, and whatever kind of cell, every cell division has the same two parts. First the cell copies its DNA. Then it hands one copy to each daughter cell.
3Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes
Every living thing belongs to one of three domains. Two of them, bacteria and archaea, are prokaryotes; the third is the eukaryotes. Which group an organism is in tells you where its DNA is and how its cells divide.
4Binary fission, mitosis and meiosis
There are three kinds of cell division. Which one a cell uses depends on whether it is a prokaryote or a eukaryote, and, in eukaryotes, on whether it is a body cell or a germ cell.
7Binary fission, step by step
Bacteria and archaea divide by binary fission. It has the same two jobs, replication and segregation, and it is the simplest way to do them.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 2

Eukaryotic chromosomes and the cell cycle

What is a eukaryotic chromosome, and what happens to it before a cell divides?

3One chromosome, then its partner: a homologous pair
Before looking at all 46, look at one. Follow one chromosome, then meet its partner from your other parent. That pair is the pattern every other chromosome follows.
2The life cycle: interphase, mitosis, then meiosis
Before zooming into each stage, walk the whole journey once with one pair of chromosomes: from fertilization, through interphase and mitosis (which build a body), to a germ cell's interphase, meiosis I and meiosis II (which make gametes), and on to the next generation. The counter under each step shows exactly when the numbers change.
1Interphase: grow, copy, get ready (G1, S, G2)
Before a eukaryotic body cell divides by mitosis, it spends most of its life in interphase, getting ready. Interphase has three stages: G1 (grow), S (copy the DNA) and G2 (get ready). The dividing itself, mitosis, comes in Part 3.
2Chromosome condensation
The DNA in one nucleus is 1 to 2 meters long, far wider than the cell, so it is always packed with proteins to fit. During interphase the cell is using its genes, so the DNA is spread out. Only when the cell is about to divide does each chromosome coil up much tighter, into a compact shape you can see, so it does not tangle as it is pulled apart.
3Counting chromosomes and the DNA molecules inside them
A chromosome is made of DNA: one DNA molecule (plus proteins) before S phase, two identical ones after. So the two counts can differ. Exam questions turn on this one rule: a replicated chromosome is still one chromosome, made of two DNA molecules.
2Sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, genes and alleles
Most of your cells have two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Keep three ideas apart: sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, and alleles.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 3

Mitosis, ploidy and the karyotype

How does mitosis share the copies, and how can you tell what kind of cell you are looking at?

1Mitosis: the drawings to know
Exam questions ask you to draw the same cell at a few moments: before DNA replication, after it, at metaphase, at anaphase, and as the two daughter cells. Here is that set for the cell from the cell cycle step, with every chromosome drawn as what it really is: DNA. Follow the molecules: one per chromosome in G1, two per chromosome after S, and one per chromosome again in each daughter cell. Prophase and telophase are left out here; to see every stage, tap through the complete cycle in Part 2.
3Haploid vs. diploid cells
Haploid and diploid are about how many sets of chromosomes a cell has. A set is one of every type. Gametes (eggs and sperm) have one set: haploid, n. Somatic cells (every other body cell) have two sets, one from each parent: diploid, 2n. That's true whether the chromosomes are unreplicated or replicated: the question is whether each type has a separate partner. Sister chromatids don't count as a second set, because they are the same chromosome copied.
1The karyotype: 46 chromosomes, 23 types
Now the whole human set. Most human cells have 46 chromosomes, but they aren't 46 of the same thing: they are 23 different types, two of each. Biologists tell the types apart by three things: size, where the centromere sits, and their pattern of stained bands.
4Chromosome numbers across species
Humans have 46, but the number isn't a rule of life: every species has its own. What stays the same is the pattern: body cells have 2n (two sets), gametes have n (one set). Click through.
6Mitosis in a life cycle (and where meiosis fits)
Mitosis and meiosis are two separate processes with two different jobs, happening at different points in a life. Mitosis copies cells (2n → 2n) to build and repair your body, all your life. Meiosis halves the number (2n → n), only in germ cells, only to make eggs and sperm for the next generation. Follow the loop from the start.

INTERACTIVE · FOUR SCENES

One process, four jobs

Tap a button to explore
1 · ONE-CELLED ORGANISMSDivision is reproductionFor a unicellular organism, such as a bacterium or a yeast, dividing in two is making offspring. Each daughter cell is a new organism.

INTERACTIVE · WHERE, WHAT SHAPE, AND HOW IT FITS

Where is the DNA?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
WHERE · PROKARYOTESOne place: loose in the cellA bacterium or archaeon has no nucleus. Its DNA sits in the cytoplasm, held on the cell membrane. Almost all its genes are on one circular chromosome.Plasmids are small extra circles of DNA, usually with genes that are not essential, such as one for resisting an antibiotic.
WHERE · EUKARYOTESThree places, two shapesThe nucleus holds most of the DNA, as linear chromosomes: this is the nuclear DNA, what "genome" usually means.Mitochondria, and the chloroplasts of plants and algae, each hold their own small circle of DNA. They came from bacteria long ago by endosymbiosis (Module 2.2), which is why their DNA is circular and they still divide by binary fission.
HOW IT FITS · ZOOM INNucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene: one inside the otherThese are not four separate places. They are zoom levels of the same thing.The nucleus holds the chromosomes. A chromosome is the name for one long double-stranded DNA molecule together with the proteins it is wound on. In a cell, DNA is always on its proteins; only how tightly it is packed changes. A gene is one stretch of that DNA, and one chromosome carries many genes.
OVER TIME · THE CELL CYCLESame DNA, different packingStages change how the DNA is packed, not where it is. Between divisions (interphase) the chromosomes are long, loose threads, so genes can be read and the DNA copied.Before the cell divides they condense: each molecule coils up into a short, compact chromosome that is easy to move. INFOGRAPHIC 6
THREE KINDS OF ORGANISM

Who divides how?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
PROKARYOTES · BACTERIA AND ARCHAEABinary fission, and that's itA bacterium or an archaeon is unicellular: one cell is the whole organism. To reproduce, it copies its DNA and splits in two by binary fission. That is asexual reproduction: one parent, two identical offspring.Prokaryotes have no nucleus and never do mitosis or meiosis.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE SEXUALLYMitosis and meiosis in the same bodyIn an animal or a flowering plant, the somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis: 2 identical cells, for growth and repair. Only the germ cells (in ovaries and testes, or in flowers) divide by meiosis: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes, all different.Here mitosis is not reproduction. Reproduction is meiosis (to make gametes) plus fertilization, a gamete from each of two parents.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE ASEXUALLYMitosis only, no meiosisMany eukaryotes also make offspring by mitosis alone: yeast grows buds, a strawberry plant sends out runners, and female aphids have young without mating. One parent, no mate, and the offspring are clones.Many species do both, depending on conditions (strawberries also flower). So prokaryotes are always asexual, but eukaryotes can be asexual, sexual or both.

MITOSIS · EUKARYOTESSomatic (body) cellsWho: eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists), in their somatic (body) cells. In a eukaryote that reproduces asexually, mitosis is also how it makes offspring.The DNA: several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent (2n → 2n), for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
MEIOSIS · EUKARYOTESGerm cells onlyWho: eukaryotes that reproduce sexually, and only in germ cells, the cells that make eggs and sperm. The same organism does mitosis in all its other cells: that is why the dashed box joins the two.Two divisions in a row: meiosis I splits each homologous pair (A from a) into 2 cells; meiosis II splits the sister chromatids, like mitosis, into 4 gametes. No DNA copying in between.The DNA: linear chromosomes in a nucleus, in homologous pairs (A from the mother, a from the father).Result: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes (2n → n) and different DNA, for sexual reproduction. How it works is Module 3.2.
ALL THREETwo categories, same two jobsBinary fission is its own category (prokaryotes). Mitosis and meiosis belong together (eukaryotes). Each one replicates the DNA and then segregates the copies. Binary fission segregates by the cell growing; mitosis and meiosis need a spindle to pull chromosomes apart.
TAP ONEWhich cells do which?Prokaryotes do only binary fission. Eukaryotes do mitosis and meiosis, never binary fission (except inside their mitochondria and chloroplasts).
Binary fission, step by step
INFOGRAPHIC 8
INTERACTIVE · SIX STEPS

One bacterium becomes two

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
1 · BEFOREDNA attached to the membraneThe circular chromosome is one DNA molecule: two strands twisted around each other, joined end to end in a circle. A protein holds it to the inside of the cell membrane.
2 · REPLICATION BEGINSCopying runs both ways roundReplication starts at one spot on the circle, the origin of replication, and runs in both directions around it.The growing copy (light) gets its own protein, attached to the membrane right next to the first one: two attachment sites, close together.
3 · COPIEDTwo circles, side by sideWhen the two copying points meet on the far side, there are two whole circles, each attached to the membrane near the other.Strictly, each circle is one original strand plus one new strand, with the same sequence. The two colors just let you follow the two circles.
4 · SEGREGATION BY GROWTHThe cell lengthensAs the cell grows longer, the two attachment sites move apart, carrying the two circles to opposite ends. Growth itself does the separating.
5 · CONSTRICTIONPinching in at the middleWhen the cell is about twice its original size and the circles are well apart, a ring of the protein FtsZ forms at the midpoint and the cell pinches in there.
6 · DIVISIONTwo daughter cellsNew membrane and cell wall are built across the middle, separating two daughter cells. Each has a complete copy of the DNA: the same genetic material as the parent cell.

Part 2 · Eukaryotic chromosomes and the cell cycle

One chromosome, then its partner: a homologous pair
INFOGRAPHIC 9
INTERACTIVE · 4 STEPS · CHROMOSOME 7

One chromosome, then a pair

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
ONE CHROMOSOMEOne long DNA moleculeA chromosome is one long DNA molecule, wrapped and packed with proteins. This is chromosome 7, the one you got from your mother. The pinch is its centromere.
ITS GENESEach at its own locusAlong that DNA sit many genes, each at a fixed position: its locus. Three are marked here, called A, B and D.
ITS PARTNERChromosome 7 from your fatherYou also got a chromosome 7 from your father. It has the same length, the same centromere position, and the same genes at the same loci.
THE PAIRA homologous pairTogether they are a homologous pair (homologs). Same genes, but each parent's version, its allele, can differ (A from mom, a from dad) or match (B and B).You have 23 pairs like this, one of each pair from each parent. The whole set, the karyotype, comes in Part 3.
The life cycle: interphase, mitosis, then meiosis
INFOGRAPHIC 10
INTERACTIVE · 19 STEPS · ONE CHROMOSOME PAIR

From fertilization to the next generation

Use Next to walk through all 19 steps
1 · FERTILIZATIONStart: one egg + one spermAn egg (one set of chromosomes, n) fuses with a sperm (one set, n). The new cell, the zygote, has two sets (2n): pink with allele A from the mother, blue with allele a from the father.The two sit side by side as a homologous pair. They never fuse into one chromosome. We follow just this one pair all the way round.
2 · INTERPHASE · G1Interphase is its own stageInterphase is not part of mitosis or meiosis. It is the time between divisions, when the cell lives and works: G1, then S, then G2.In G1 the DNA is loose, still wrapped on its proteins, so the cell can read its genes. 2 chromosomes = 2 DNA molecules.
3 · INTERPHASE · SCopied while looseS phase: each chromosome is copied into two identical sister chromatids held at the centromere. The DNA is still loose: copying needs it open.Count centromeres: still 2 chromosomes. Count chromatids: now 4 DNA molecules. Sisters match (A A, a a).
4 · INTERPHASE · G2Ready to divideStill loose, already copied. The cell grows and gets ready. Interphase ends here, and the division begins.
5 · MITOSIS · PROPHASEWinds up tightOnly now does the DNA wind up tight into compact chromosomes, so they can be moved without tangling.In mitosis each chromosome acts on its own: partners never pair up and nothing is swapped.
6 · MITOSIS · METAPHASESingle fileThe chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell. Each one's sisters are still joined (A with A, a with a).
7 · MITOSIS · ANAPHASESisters pulled apartThe sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends. Each side gets one A and one a. Once apart, each chromatid counts as a chromosome of its own (that is the 4).
8 · MITOSIS · TELOPHASE2 identical cells, not gametesA nucleus forms around each set, the DNA loosens again, and cytokinesis splits the cell.Result of mitosis: 2 identical body cells, each Aa and 2n. Mitosis never makes gametes. Each new cell starts again at G1.
9 · GROWSteps 2 to 8, millions of timesInterphase then mitosis, over and over, builds the whole body. Every cell has the same pair. Most stay body cells forever and never do meiosis.A few, in the ovaries or testes, are germ cells (gold). They are 2n, made by mitosis too, and can do more mitosis. Only they will ever do meiosis.
10 · GERM CELL · INTERPHASEOne copy for all of meiosisWe follow one germ cell (not a gamete). It goes through G1, S and G2 exactly as before, DNA loose the whole time.This S phase is the only copying for the whole of meiosis. There is none between meiosis I and meiosis II.
11 · MEIOSIS I · PROPHASE IPartners pair and cross overMeiosis I begins at prophase I. The DNA winds up tight, and the two partners (homologs) pair up side by side, the only time they ever pair.A pink and a blue chromatid swap pieces where they cross (the gold ring): crossing over. It happens between partners, never between sisters.
12 · MEIOSIS I · METAPHASE IPairs line up togetherThe pairs line up together in the middle, partners on opposite sides. Which partner faces which side is random for every pair: that is independent assortment.
13 · MEIOSIS I · ANAPHASE IPartners pulled apartThe partners are pulled apart: pink one way, blue the other. The sisters stay joined. This is segregation, and the step that halves the chromosome number.
14 · MEIOSIS I · TELOPHASE I2 cells, each n, still doubledThe cell splits into 2. Each has one chromosome of this type, so each is haploid (n), even though that chromosome is still two chromatids: ploidy counts chromosomes (centromeres), not DNA molecules.These are not gametes. The DNA only loosens slightly, and no S phase comes next.
15 · MEIOSIS II · PROPHASE IIBoth cells, no copyingProphase II happens in both cells at once. The chromosomes tighten fully again. Meiosis II works like mitosis, but starts from haploid cells and without copying first.
16 · MEIOSIS II · METAPHASE IISingle file againIn each cell the chromosome lines up single file, sisters on opposite sides, as in mitosis.
17 · MEIOSIS II · ANAPHASE IISisters pulled apartThe sisters are pulled apart in both cells. Each separated chromatid now counts as a chromosome of its own.
18 · MEIOSIS II · TELOPHASE II4 gametesThe DNA loosens fully and 4 haploid gametes form, all different: 2 unmixed, 2 mixed by crossing over. One person makes only eggs or only sperm (a pea flower makes both).Gametes are the end of the line: they never divide again.
19 · FERTILIZATION · NEXT GENERATIONBack to the startAfter meiosis II is finished, one gamete meets one from a different person: 1 + 1 = 1 zygote. That zygote is the next generation, and it starts again at step 1.
Interphase: grow, copy, get ready (G1, S, G2)
INFOGRAPHIC 11
INTERACTIVE · 3 STAGES · ONE CELL

Interphase in one cell

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
G1 · GAP 1GrowThe cell grows, makes proteins and does its normal job. Each chromosome is unreplicated: one DNA molecule. This cell has 4: a long pair (A from mom, a from dad) and a short pair (B and B).
S · DNA SYNTHESISCopy every chromosomeEach chromosome's DNA is copied. The copy stays attached at the centromere, so each chromosome is now two sister chromatids.Still 4 chromosomes, but now 8 DNA molecules. (In a real cell the DNA stays unspooled the whole time; it's drawn short so you can follow it.)
G2 · GAP 2Get readyThe cell grows a little more and builds what it needs to divide. Every chromosome is two identical sisters: A and A, a and a, B and B.Next, the cell divides by mitosis (Part 3).
Chromosome condensation
INFOGRAPHIC 12
INTERACTIVE · ONE CHROMOSOME, THREE STATES

From thread to package

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
INTERPHASE · BEFORE SA long, open threadThe chromosome is one long DNA molecule, unspooled so the cell can read its genes. Chromosomes are not visible under a microscope now.
INTERPHASE · AFTER SCopied, still openAfter replication there are two identical DNA molecules: gene 1 and an exact copy of gene 1. They are still unspooled.
START OF MITOSISPacked up to moveThe two molecules condense into a compact replicated chromosome: two sister chromatids held together at the centromere. Packed this way, they can be moved without tangling.
Counting chromosomes and the DNA molecules inside them
INFOGRAPHIC 13
INTERACTIVE · COUNT BEFORE AND AFTER

Count centromeres, then count chromatids

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
BEFORE S PHASE1 chromosome, 1 DNA moleculeAn unreplicated chromosome: one centromere, one DNA molecule.
AFTER S PHASEStill 1 chromosome, now 2 DNA moleculesReplication doubled the DNA but not the number of chromosomes: there is still one centromere, so it is one chromosome, made of two sister chromatids.
AFTER THE SISTERS SEPARATENow each chromatid is a chromosomeWhen mitosis pulls the sisters apart, each one has its own centromere and counts as a full chromosome.
Sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, genes and alleles
INFOGRAPHIC 14
INTERACTIVE · TWO PAIRS AFTER S PHASE

Same allele or different?

Tap a button to explore
SISTER CHROMATIDSAlways the same alleleSister chromatids are copies made by replication in S phase, so they carry the same allele of every gene: A and A. That is true for every pair of sisters, unless a new mutation happened.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESA pair, one from each parentTwo chromosomes carrying the same set of genes: one inherited from your mother, one from your father. Their DNA is nearly identical, not identical, so their alleles can differ.
DIFFERENT ALLELES · A AND aSame gene, two versionsThe long pair carries the same gene at the same place, but the mother's version is A and the father's is a. Two different alleles of one gene.
THE SAME ALLELE · B AND BSame gene, same versionThe short pair carries B from the mother and B from the father. The homologs still came from two parents, but here they happen to carry the same allele.
TAP A LABELCopies always match; pairs may notA gene is a stretch of DNA carrying the information for one product. An allele is one version of that gene. Tap each label to see when two alleles are the same and when they differ.

Part 3 · Mitosis, ploidy and the karyotype

Mitosis: the drawings to know
INFOGRAPHIC 15
INTERACTIVE · ONE CELL, EVERY DNA MOLECULE

From one cell to two, molecule by molecule

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
INTERPHASE · G1Each chromosome is one DNA moleculeEvery chromosome is one double-stranded DNA molecule: two strands twisted around each other. This cell has 4: a long pair (A from the mother, a from the father) and a short pair (B and B).4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules. In the real cell each one is a long, loose thread; they are drawn short so you can see the two strands.
INTERPHASE · SDNA replication: one molecule becomes twoZoom in on chromosome A. Its two strands come apart, and each one is the template for a new partner strand (dashed).The result is two DNA molecules, each one original strand and one new strand, held together at the centromere. They are the two sister chromatids, and both carry allele A: two copies of the same allele.In the real cell the strands come apart a little at a time, at many spots at once, and the new strand is built right behind the opening. The drawing splits it into two moments so you can see it.
INTERPHASE · G2Every chromosome is now two moleculesAll 4 chromosomes were copied the same way. Each is now two sister chromatids joined at one centromere: A and A, a and a, B and B, B and B.Still 4 chromosomes (count the centromeres), but 8 DNA molecules (count the chromatids).
M PHASE · METAPHASELine up in the middleProphase has coiled each chromosome up (shorter here). Now each replicated chromosome lines up separately in the middle of the cell, with spindle fibers from both poles attached at its centromere, so one sister faces each pole.Still 4 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules.
M PHASE · ANAPHASEThe two molecules separateThe centromeres split and the spindle pulls the two DNA molecules of every chromosome to opposite poles. Each molecule is now its own chromosome.For a moment the cell holds 8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules: A, a, B and B on each side.
AFTER TELOPHASE + CYTOKINESISTwo daughter cells, identical to the parentTelophase builds a nucleus around each set, and cytokinesis splits the cell in two. Each daughter has 4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules, alleles A a B B: exactly what the parent had in G1.Each molecule is one original strand and one new strand, but the sequence is the same, so the copies are identical. Each daughter starts again in G1.
INFOGRAPHIC 16
STEP THROUGH IT · ONE COLOR PER CHROMOSOME

Mitosis keeps the number

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
PROPHASE5 chromosomes, 10 DNA moleculesEach chromosome was copied in S phase, so each is two identical sister chromatids. One color per chromosome makes each one easy to follow.
METAPHASESingle fileEach replicated chromosome lines up on its own in the middle. Sisters are still joined, so the count hasn't changed.
ANAPHASEEvery pair of sisters splitsOne copy of every color goes to each pole. For a moment the cell holds 10 chromosomes.
TWO DAUGHTERSOne of each color: 5 againEach daughter gets one copy of all 5 chromosomes. Mitosis undoes the copying; it never halves the number.
Haploid vs. diploid cells
INFOGRAPHIC 17
INTERACTIVE · 4 STEPS · ONE SET OR TWO

Gametes vs. somatic cells, replicated or not

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
HAPLOID · ONE SETA gameteAn egg or sperm holds one complete set: one chromosome of each type, every one different in length, centromere position and bands. In this sketch n = 4; in humans n = 23.
DIPLOID · TWO SETSA somatic cellA somatic cell has the same types, but each type has a separate matching partner: one set from the mother (pink), one from the father (blue). 2n = 8 here, 46 in humans.
REPLICATED · STILL HAPLOIDCopies aren't partnersAfter replication each chromosome is two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. There is still only one chromosome of each type, so the cell is still haploid. Sister chromatids are the same chromosome copied.
REPLICATED · STILL DIPLOIDCount separate chromosomesA somatic cell after S phase still has two separate chromosomes of each type, each now two sisters. Still diploid. The quick test: pick one type and count the centromeres. One → haploid. Two → diploid.
INFOGRAPHIC 18
INTERACTIVE · ONE SET OR TWO, STEP BY STEP

Think of the chromosomes as a set of books

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
HAPLOID · ONE SET (n)One copy of each kind of chromosomePicture the chromosomes as a set of instruction books: book 1, book 2, book 3, each with different genes. A haploid cell has one complete set: one copy of each book.n is the number of different kinds of chromosomes in one set. This egg has n = 3. In humans, n = 23.
DIPLOID · TWO SETS (2n)Two copies of each kind, one from each parentA diploid cell has two complete sets: one set came from the mother's egg (pink), the other from the father's sperm (blue). So every kind of chromosome is there twice.The two copies of one kind are a homologous pair. This cell is 2n = 6: three pairs. Your body cells are 2n = 46: 23 pairs.
HOMOLOGS · SAME BOOK, TWO EDITIONSSame genes, maybe different allelesThe two homologs carry the same genes in the same places, like two editions of one book with the same chapters. The wording of a chapter can differ: those versions are alleles (A from mom, a from dad).So a diploid cell has two alleles of every gene (they may match or differ), and a haploid cell has one.
THE TRAP · COPYING DOESN'T ADD A SETA photocopy isn't a second editionIn S phase each chromosome is copied, and the copy stays stuck to it as a sister chromatid, like photocopying book 1 and clipping the copy to the original. You still have only book 1 from one parent: no new type, no edition from the other parent.A second set means a second chromosome of every type from the other parent, and that only comes from fertilization. So copying never changes ploidy: this haploid cell is still haploid (n = 3) after S.
IN HUMANS23 or 46Egg: n = 23. Sperm: n = 23. Fertilization: n + n = 2n = 46, the zygote. Mitosis then copies those 46 into every body cell.Only the gametes are haploid. They are made by meiosis, which halves 46 to 23 (Module 3.2).
INFOGRAPHIC 19
PRACTICE · SORT FIVE CELLS

Haploid or diploid?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
CELL 1 · HAPLOID, n = 3No pairsThree chromosomes, every one different. One set, so haploid.
CELL 2 · DIPLOID, 2n = 6Three pairsEach chromosome has a match of the same length and genes: three homologous pairs, two sets. Diploid.
CELL 3 · HAPLOID, n = 2Replicated, but still no pairsTwo replicated chromosomes that are different from each other. Being replicated does not make a cell diploid: the two sisters are copies, not a pair. Haploid.
CELL 4 · HAPLOID, n = 3Read the genesIn metaphase the chromosomes carry genes g, e and f. Each gene appears on only one chromosome (twice, on its two sisters), so there are no homologous pairs. Haploid.
CELL 5 · CAN'T TELLTwo chromosomes, no labelsFrom the number alone, you can't tell. If the two are homologs carrying the same genes, it is diploid (2n = 2). If they carry different genes, it is haploid (n = 2).
The karyotype: 46 chromosomes, 23 types
INFOGRAPHIC 20
INTERACTIVE · 8 STEPS · A HUMAN KARYOTYPE

From a messy spread to 23 pairs

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 8
UNDER THE MICROSCOPENot neat X'sStop a cell in mitosis, squash it flat and stain it, and this is what you see: 46 bent, fuzzy, overlapping shapes. Diagrams draw tidy X's; real chromosomes look wonky.They're replicated at this point: each is two sister chromatids held tight at the centromere, which is why diagrams draw them as X's. See a real one: the National Human Genome Research Institute's karyotype.
THE KARYOTYPESorted into pairsPhotograph the chromosomes, then line them up in pairs: that's a karyotype, the textbook's "portrait formed by the number and shapes of chromosomes." 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs.The two chromosomes of a pair are homologous chromosomes (homologs). A karyotype is one picture of a cell's whole set; a homologous pair is two chromosomes inside it.
SIZENumbered longest to shortest (almost)The 22 numbered pairs go from the longest (chromosome 1) down to the shortest.One surprise: when they were named, 22 looked like the smallest, but 21 is actually a little shorter than 22. So it's "roughly" by size.
CENTROMERE POSITIONWhere the pinch isThe centromere sits in a fixed spot for each type: near the middle (chromosome 1), off-center (4) or near one end (13). Same length can still mean different types.
BANDSA barcode for each typeA stain gives every type its own pattern of dark and light bands. Both members of a pair have the same length, centromere and bands: that's how the pairs are matched.
AUTOSOMES22 types, 22 sets of genesPairs 1 to 22 are the autosomes. Each type carries a different set of genes; that's why the types aren't interchangeable.
SEX CHROMOSOMESThe 23rd pair: X and YThe 23rd pair are the sex chromosomes: XX in genetic females, XY in genetic males (this karyotype is male).X and Y are the important exception: a different size and different genes, so they are a pair that doesn't match. Every other pair matches.
LOCUSA gene's addressA locus (Latin for place; plural loci) is a gene's position on a chromosome. Same word as "locus of control" in psychology, where you feel control is located; here it's where a gene is located.Both homologs have the same gene at the same locus. The version sitting at that address, the allele, can differ: A on one, a on the other.

INTERACTIVE · 8 SPECIES · 2n AND n

Same pattern, different numbers

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 8
FRUIT FLY · 2n = 8, n = 4Fruit flyBody cells: 8 chromosomes in 4 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 4, one of each type. Drosophila melanogaster: the fly geneticists use.
GARDEN PEA · 2n = 14, n = 7Garden peaBody cells: 14 chromosomes in 7 pairs. Eggs and sperm: 7, one of each type. Pisum sativum: Mendel's plant.

Mitosis in a life cycle (and where meiosis fits)
INFOGRAPHIC 22
INTERACTIVE · 5 STEPS · THE HUMAN LIFE CYCLE

A loop with a start: where mitosis and meiosis each happen

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
START HERE · THE ZYGOTEYou began as one cellEvery person starts as one cell, the zygote: diploid (2n), with one set of chromosomes from mom's egg and one from dad's sperm.
MITOSIS · ALL YOUR LIFECopy, then share, again and againThe zygote divides by mitosis, and so do its daughters, again and again: that's how you grow and how you repair. Every cell made this way is 2n with the same DNA. This is the division this module is about.
GERM CELLSA few cells set asideMost of your cells are somatic (skin, gut, blood). A few are germ cells, kept in the gonads (ovaries or testes). They're 2n too, and mitosis made them like every other cell.
MEIOSIS · ONLY HEREGerm cells make gametesMeiosis is a different division with a different job: it happens only in germ cells, and only to make gametes (eggs or sperm). It halves the number: 2n → n. That's Module 3.2.
FERTILIZATIONBack to the startAn egg (n) and a sperm (n) fuse: n + n = 2n, a new zygote, the start of the next generation. The loop begins again.
INFOGRAPHIC 23
SCENE · DIFFERENT CELLS, SAME DNA

Does a skin cell have different DNA from a liver cell?

No. Every somatic cell came from the same zygote by mitosis, so they all have the same DNA, except for any new mutations. Cells differ in which genes they use, not in which genes they have.

Why cells divide, and binary fission
